name: Notch Flow Adjustable Rope Wrench
title: Notch Flow Adjustable Rope Wrench for SRS Climbing
meta: The Notch Flow adjustable rope wrench tunes friction for SRS climbing on a hitch. How it works, who it suits, setup tips and what to inspect before you climb.
tagline: An adjustable rope wrench for SRS climbers who want to dial friction to the rope.
summary: The Notch Flow is a notch rope wrench with adjustable friction, built to sit above a friction hitch on a stationary rope system. It lets you tune how much bite the wrench adds so descents stay smooth on fresh, stiff or worn rope.
highlights: Adjustable friction for different ropes and climber weights
Works above a friction hitch in an SRS setup
Smooth, controllable descents on a single line
Tether connects the wrench to the hitch system
Fits common arborist climbing line diameters (check the manual for range)

p: A fixed rope wrench gives the same friction on every rope. That is fine until you switch from a slick, new line to a fuzzy one that has seen a season of pine pitch, or until a lighter climber borrows your kit. The Flow lets you move the friction up or down so the hitch does the fine control and the wrench takes the heavy work.
On a long descent from a big removal, that adjustability is the difference between feeding rope with both hands and gliding down with one hand on the hitch.
It also helps on short, choppy descents through a crown. With the friction set right, you can stop, reposition and start again without the hitch grabbing or slipping.

The Flow rides above your hitch on a short tether and needs to be set up exactly as Notch shows in the instructions, with the tether length matched to your hitch. Check the friction surfaces for grooves, the tether for wear and the connection points for damage before each climb. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
Pair it with a hitch cord and climbing line from our SRS devices range and practice low before you trust it high.

faq.q: Can I use the Notch Flow on MRS?
faq.a: It is designed for SRS, where the rope is fixed and the climber moves on it. Follow the manufacturer's instructions for approved configurations.

faq.q: Do I still need a friction hitch?
faq.a: Yes. A rope wrench works together with a friction hitch. The wrench adds friction and keeps the hitch tending smoothly; it does not replace it.

name: Kong Duck Emergency Belay Device
title: Kong Duck Ascender and Emergency Rope Clamp
h1: Kong Duck Ascender and Emergency Belay Device
meta: The Kong Duck ascender is a tiny rope clamp for emergency belays, hauling and backup ascending. What it does in a tree kit, limits, and how to inspect it.
tagline: A pocket-size Kong rope clamp for emergency ascending, hauling and rescue backup.
summary: The Kong Duck ascender is a compact, handle-free rope clamp that climbers carry for emergency ascending, short hauls and rescue setups. It weighs next to nothing, clips to a gear loop and goes on the rope without taking anything else off it.
highlights: Very small and light, easy to carry every day
Clamps onto the rope mid-line without untying anything
Useful for emergency ascents, mechanical advantage hauls and backups
Simple aluminum and steel construction with few parts
Works with the carabiner you already carry
Fits a wide range of rope diameters (check the markings)

p: The Duck is the clamp you forget about until the day you need it. It is small enough to live on your saddle permanently, and it goes onto the rope in seconds. Climbers use it to build a quick foot loop for an emergency ascent, to grab a rope for a short mechanical advantage haul, or to add a backup in a rescue setup.
Because it has no handle, it is not a replacement for a full handled ascender on a long rope walk. Think of it as a utility clamp and a get-out-of-trouble tool.

Tree crews that train for aerial rescue often carry a Duck alongside a pulley and a few slings. With a pulley like the one on the Petzl Rollclip, it turns into a simple hauling system to take weight off a stuck or injured climber's line.
The value is in having it with you and knowing how to use it. Practice the systems you plan to use on the ground with a qualified trainer before you rely on them aloft.

A small toothed cam can damage a rope if it is shock loaded, so keep slack out of any system built on the Duck and never use it where a fall onto it is possible unless the manufacturer specifically allows that configuration.

Check the cam teeth for wear and packed debris, make sure the spring snaps the cam back, and look for cracks or sharp edges on the body. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
If the Duck has been loaded hard, for example in a rescue or a haul that shock loaded, inspect it closely before carrying it again and retire it if you have any doubt.

body.h: Where it sits in your kit
p: Most climbers clip the Duck to a rear gear loop with a dedicated locking carabiner so it is always in the same place. It weighs so little that there is no reason to leave it in the truck.

Pair it with a short sewn sling or a prusik loop as a foot loop, a small pulley and a spare locking carabiner, and you have the core of an emergency ascent or a simple haul. If you ever need to get off a stuck system, climb past a jammed hitch or lift a co-worker's weight, those few pieces cover a lot of problems.

On the ground it earns its keep too. Use it to put a little tension on a tag line, to hold a pull line while you take a wrap on a tree, or to grab a rope when you need a hand-hold for a short haul of brush up a bank.

faq.q: Is the Kong Duck a full ascender?
faq.a: It is a compact rope clamp. It can be used for ascending, but it has no handle, so most climbers treat it as an emergency and utility tool rather than their main ascender.

faq.q: What rope sizes does the Duck fit?
faq.a: It covers a wide range of common climbing line diameters. Check the markings on your device and Kong's instructions for the exact range.

faq.q: Can I use it for hauling?
faq.a: Yes, it is commonly used as the rope grab in simple mechanical advantage hauls. Keep the system slack-free and follow the manufacturer's limits.

faq.q: How do I check it?
faq.a: Inspect the cam teeth, spring action, axle and body before each use. Retire it if teeth are worn flat, the spring is weak or the body is cracked or deformed.

name: ART Positioner Replacement Cam
title: ART Positioner Replacement Cam
meta: Replacement cam for the ART Positioner lanyard adjuster. When to swap the position cam, how to check wear, and why genuine ART parts matter on climbing gear.
tagline: A genuine replacement cam to keep your ART Positioner lanyard adjuster working right.
summary: This is the replacement position cam for the ART Positioner, the lanyard adjuster many climbers run on their flipline. When the cam's gripping surface wears, swapping it brings the adjuster back to spec without buying a whole new unit.
highlights: Genuine ART part for the Positioner
Restores grip when the old cam is worn
Cheaper than replacing the whole adjuster
Keeps a trusted lanyard setup in service

p: The cam is what grips your lanyard rope, and it wears every time you adjust. Signs it is due include slipping under load, polished or flattened gripping surfaces, and a lanyard that creeps when you lean back on a spur climb.
Because the Positioner is life-support gear, do not wait until it slips badly. Replace the cam when the wear starts to show and keep the old one out of the kit.

Dirty rope speeds up wear. Sand, grit and dried sap act like sandpaper on the cam every time the lanyard slides through it. Climbers who work in sandy soil or heavy pine sap often see wear sooner than those in clean hardwoods, so set your inspection schedule by your conditions, not by the calendar.

Install the cam exactly as ART describes, using only genuine parts. After the swap, test the adjuster close to the ground with full body weight before you climb on it. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
If the body, axle or spring of the Positioner itself shows cracks, wear or deformation, a new cam will not fix it. Retire the unit and look at our rope grabs instead.
Keep the old cam out of circulation once it is replaced. Mark it or bin it so it cannot end up back in a kit by mistake, and note the date of the swap in your gear log if your company keeps one.

faq.q: Will this cam fit other lanyard adjusters?
faq.a: No. It is made for the ART Positioner. Use the correct genuine part for any other device.

faq.q: How often should the cam be replaced?
faq.a: It depends on how much you climb and how dirty your rope is. Inspect it before each climb and replace it when wear affects grip.

name: Climb Right Rope Grab
title: Climb Right Rope Grab for Lanyards and Positioning
meta: The Climb Right rope grab adds a simple cam adjuster for gripping rope on a lanyard or positioning line. What it does, where it fits, and how to inspect it.
tagline: A simple cam-style rope grab for adjusting a lanyard or positioning line.
summary: The Climb Right rope grab is a cam-style device for gripping rope on a lanyard or a secondary positioning line. Slide it to adjust, load it and it holds, so you can set your distance from the stem with one hand.
highlights: One-handed adjustment on a positioning lanyard
Cam design that grips under load
Compact and easy to clip on a saddle
A practical, budget-friendly adjuster

p: Most climbers use a rope grab like this on a rope lanyard, so they can shorten up to lean back on a spar or let out length to reach around a big stem. Gripping rope with a cam is faster than retying a hitch and easier with gloves on.
It also works for holding a light load on a short line or tensioning a tag line on the ground.

On spur work and removals, being able to snug up your position quickly matters. A cam grab lets you take up slack as the stem narrows without stopping to retie anything, which keeps the job moving and your hands on the work.

Match the device to the rope diameter it is marked for. A cam on rope that is too thin can slip, and on rope that is too fat it may not close properly. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
If you want a device that is built into a complete lanyard, compare it with the Petzl Zillon.

Before each climb, check the cam teeth for wear and packed debris, make sure the spring returns the cam crisply, and look for cracks or deformation on the body and the attachment hole. Test it on the ground with full weight before going up, and retire it if it ever slips under load.

faq.q: Can a rope grab be my primary climbing device?
faq.a: Only if the manufacturer rates it for that use. Most lanyard rope grabs are for work positioning, not as the main climbing system.

faq.q: What rope should I use with it?
faq.a: Use rope within the diameter range marked on the device and listed in the instructions.

name: Petzl Micrograb Lanyard Adjuster
title: Petzl Micrograb Lanyard Adjuster Rope Grab
h1: Petzl Micrograb Rope Grab Lanyard Adjuster
meta: The Petzl Micrograb is a compact Petzl rope grab for adjusting a tree-care positioning lanyard. How it works, rope fit and inspection basics for climbers.
tagline: A compact Petzl rope grab for adjusting a tree-care positioning lanyard.
summary: The Petzl Micrograb is a compact Petzl rope grab that turns a length of arborist rope into an adjustable work-positioning lanyard. It grips the rope with a cam and releases with a simple pull, so you can take up or let out slack on the stem.
highlights: Compact cam adjuster made for tree-care lanyards
Easy one-handed adjustment
Works with a length of compatible arborist rope
Good option for building your own lanyard length
specs: Compatible arborist rope, per Petzl instructions

p: The Micrograb lets you choose your own lanyard length and rope. Many climbers run it on a length of 11 to 13 mm class arborist line with a sewn eye, which keeps the whole lanyard lighter than a wire core flipline. Check Petzl's notice for the exact compatible ropes before you buy rope for it.
If you would rather buy a complete kit, see the Micrograb lanyard add-on kit.

A rope lanyard built around the Micrograb is also gentler on bark than wire core, which matters on pruning jobs where you are choking limbs and repositioning often. It slides around the stem easily and coils up neatly on a saddle loop.

Look for wear on the cam, a weak return spring and cracks or deformation on the body. Rope wear behind the cam shows up first, so check the lanyard rope too. A rope lanyard is not cut resistant, so keep it away from the chainsaw or pair it with a wire core flipline when cutting. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
Keep the cam clean. Sap, sand and sawdust packed into the teeth reduce grip, so brush it out at the end of the day and let it dry before storing it in your bag.

faq.q: Is the Micrograb a fall arrest device?
faq.a: No. It is a work-positioning lanyard adjuster. Use it only within Petzl's stated uses.

faq.q: Can I use any rope with it?
faq.a: Use only rope that Petzl lists as compatible in the instructions for the Micrograb.

name: Petzl Mino Carabiner
title: Petzl Mino Carabiner for Gear Organization
meta: The Petzl Mino carabiner is a small accessory clip for racking gear on your saddle. What it is for, what it is not rated for, and smart ways to use one.
tagline: A small accessory clip for racking gear, not for life support.
summary: The Petzl Mino carabiner is a small accessory clip for organizing gear on a saddle loop or bag. It keeps slings, hitch cords and hand tools where you can find them without tying up a rated carabiner.
highlights: Small and light for racking gear
Frees up rated connectors for climbing
Easy to clip with gloves on
Not for climbing or life support

p: Every climber has a pile of small stuff that needs a home: a handsaw scabbard, spare hitch cord, a rescue pulley, a throw weight. Accessory clips like the Mino keep that stuff sorted on your saddle loops so the rated hardware stays free for the system.
They also work in the truck and in gear bags for hanging slings and lanyards so they dry and stay untangled.
Clips like this also make it easy to hand off gear. Unclip a sling from your rack and pass it to a co-climber without touching your system hardware.

body.h: Keep it out of the system
p: An accessory carabiner is not a climbing connector. Never use it in your climbing, rigging or rescue system, and keep it a different color or shape from your rated gear so nobody grabs the wrong one in a hurry. For rated connectors, browse our carabiners and hardware.

It is worth taking a few minutes to sort your rack before a big job. Put racking clips on the loops where gear hangs, rated carabiners on the bridge and side rings, and keep the two from mixing. That habit pays off when you are tired at the end of a long day and reaching for things by feel.

faq.q: Can I climb on a Petzl Mino?
faq.a: No. It is an accessory clip for organizing gear. Use a rated locking carabiner for any life-support connection.

faq.q: What does it hold best?
faq.a: Light gear such as hitch cords, slings, small pulleys and tool holders.

name: DMM Shadow Locksafe Carabiner
title: DMM Shadow Auto-Locking Carabiner for Arborists
meta: The DMM Shadow is a DMM carabiner with an auto-locking gate and keylock nose for tree climbing. Where it fits on a saddle, how to load it, and inspection tips.
tagline: A light, auto-locking DMM carabiner with a snag-free nose for everyday climbing.
summary: The DMM Shadow is a DMM carabiner with an auto-locking Locksafe gate and a keylock nose that slides through rope eyes and bridges without snagging. Climbers use it for hitch connections, lanyard ends and anywhere a dependable all-round locking connector is needed.
highlights: Auto-locking gate closes and locks on its own
Keylock nose reduces snagging on eyes and slings
Light enough to carry several on a saddle
Made by DMM in Wales
Strength ratings marked on the spine

p: DMM carabiners have a long reputation in climbing for clean gates, smooth action and tight quality control. The Shadow is a general-purpose locker that suits most connections on a modern arborist saddle: the hitch on a split tail, the end of a rope lanyard, or a pulley on the bridge.

The keylock nose matters more than people think. A notched nose can catch on a sewn eye or a rope bridge as you clip and unclip. The smooth keylock shape slides through, which means fewer fumbles when you are tied in at height.

Many climbers run a matched set of the same locking carabiner across their saddle. When every connector opens the same way, your hands learn the motion and you stop thinking about it, which counts when you are tired or working in poor light.
The Shadow is light enough that carrying several costs little. Keep one or two spares on a rear loop for redirects, a rescue pulley or a hitch that needs to be rebuilt mid-climb.

An auto-locking gate locks itself every time it closes, so you do not have to remember to screw it shut. On a climbing system that is a real safety advantage, and it is why many tree climbing standards and company policies call for self-closing, self-locking connectors in life-support positions.

Screw gates still have a place for semi-permanent connections, but for connections you open and close all day, an auto-locker like the Shadow is the better tool. Compare options in our auto-locking carabiners range.

Any carabiner is strongest when loaded along its spine, gate closed and locked. Avoid cross-loading, three-way loading and loading over an edge. Keep the gate away from tree limbs and other hardware that could push it open.
Watch for the carabiner rotating so the gate ends up against your saddle bridge or another connector. If that keeps happening, a captive-eye setup or a different arrangement may be better.

Before each climb, check that the gate closes and locks on its own, the spring is crisp, and there is no grit in the hinge or locking sleeve. Look for grooves worn by rope, sharp edges, cracks or corrosion.

Retire any carabiner that has been dropped onto a hard surface from height, shows deep wear or fails to lock reliably. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

Keep a simple record of when each carabiner went into service. It makes it easier to spot gear that has been on the saddle for years and to rotate it out before it wears thin, and many company gear programs require a log like this anyway.

faq.q: Is the DMM Shadow good for tree climbing?
faq.a: Yes. It is an auto-locking aluminum carabiner with a keylock nose, which suits most connections on an arborist saddle. Check the ratings on the spine against your company's requirements.

faq.q: How strong is it?
faq.a: Strength ratings for the major axis, minor axis and gate open are laser marked on the spine. Read them on the carabiner you buy.

faq.q: Why use auto-locking instead of screw-lock?
faq.a: An auto-locking gate locks every time it closes, so it does not rely on you remembering to screw it shut. Most climbers use auto-lockers for life-support connections.

faq.q: When should I retire a carabiner?
faq.a: Retire it after a hard drop, if it shows grooves or sharp wear from rope, cracks, deformation, or a gate that does not close and lock cleanly.

name: Petzl Am'D Triact-Lock Carabiner
title: Petzl Am'D Auto-Locking Carabiner for Tree Climbing
meta: The Petzl Am'D is the Petzl carabiner many arborists clip first: asymmetric D shape, Triact-Lock auto gate and keylock nose. Specs, uses and inspection tips.
tagline: Petzl's asymmetric D locker with a three-action auto-locking gate for climbing systems.
summary: The Petzl Am'D Triact-Lock is the Petzl carabiner a lot of arborists reach for first: an asymmetric D-shaped aluminum locker with a three-action auto-locking gate. It is strong, light and sized to hold a hitch, a pulley or a lanyard eye without crowding.
highlights: Asymmetric D shape keeps load on the spine
Triact-Lock gate locks itself and resists accidental opening
Keylock nose slides through eyes without snagging
28 kN major-axis rating
Light aluminum body suited to all-day carrying

p: The Am'D has been one of the most common Petzl climbing carabiners on tree saddles for years, and for good reason. The asymmetric D shape keeps the load close to the spine, where the carabiner is strongest, while leaving a wide opening at the gate end for rope, eyes and pulleys.
It handles split tail hitches, rope wrench tethers, lanyard eyes and rigging connections with equal ease. Many climbers run a matched set of them so every connection on the saddle behaves the same.

The aluminum frame keeps weight down, which matters once you have six or eight carabiners on a saddle. Over a full day of climbing, those ounces add up in your hips and legs, and lighter hardware is one of the easiest places to save weight without giving up strength.

The Triact-Lock gate needs three movements to open: slide, twist and push. That makes it very hard for a branch or rope to open by accident, and the gate locks itself as soon as you let go. It takes a few climbs to make the motion automatic, but after that it is quick to use with gloves.
If you want a screw gate for semi-permanent connections, the Am'D Screw-Lock uses the same frame.

Load the carabiner along its long axis with the gate closed and locked. Keep it from cross-loading against your bridge or another connector, and avoid letting the gate rest against bark or a limb where pressure could work it open.
For pulleys and hitch setups, check that the carabiner sits flat and the rope runs over the right part of the frame. A captive pin or rubber keeper can help hold orientation.

When you set up a rope wrench tether or a hitch on a split tail, make sure the Am'D sits so the rope runs over the wide end of the frame and the gate faces away from your body and the bridge. If it keeps flipping into a bad position, a rubber keeper or a captive-eye setup can hold it in place. Check orientation each time you rebuild your system.

Check gate action every time you climb. It should close fully and lock on its own. Rinse out grit, look for rope grooves, and retire any carabiner that has taken a hard drop or shows cracks or corrosion. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

Keep an eye on the gate sleeve in particular. Sap and sawdust can make a Triact-Lock sluggish, so it may not fully lock when you let go. Rinse it in warm water, dry it well and check that it snaps closed and locks on its own before the next climb.

faq.q: What are the Petzl Am'D strength ratings?
faq.a: The Am'D is rated 28 kN on the major axis, 8 kN on the minor axis and 7 kN gate open. Always confirm the markings on your carabiner.

faq.q: Triact-Lock or Screw-Lock?
faq.a: Triact-Lock locks itself and is preferred for connections you open often. Screw-Lock suits semi-permanent connections and costs a little less.

faq.q: Is the Am'D good for rigging?
faq.a: It works for light rigging connections within its ratings, but heavy rigging usually calls for steel connectors or dedicated rigging hardware.

name: Notch V3 Quickie
title: Notch V3 Quickie Climbing Hardware
meta: The Notch Quickie V3 is compact hardware for quick, semi-permanent connections in a climbing setup. What it does, where it fits, and how to check it before use.
tagline: Compact Notch hardware for quick, tidy connections in a climbing setup.
summary: The Notch Quickie V3 is a compact piece of hardware for making quick, tidy connections in a tree climbing setup. Climbers use it where a full carabiner is bulky and they want a low-profile link that stays put.
highlights: Third-generation Notch design
Low-profile alternative to a carabiner in some setups
Keeps connections tidy and oriented
Simple to inspect

p: Small connectors like the Notch V3 Quickie are about cutting clutter. Fewer bulky carabiners on a bridge or hitch setup means less cross-loading, less weight and a system that stays in the right orientation as you move through the canopy.
Use it only in the configurations shown in the Notch instructions. Hardware that works well in one position can be wrong for another.
A tidy system also makes inspection easier. When every connection sits in the same place every day, it is quicker to spot something that has moved, worn or been set up wrong.

Check for wear, cracks, deformation and any damage to the closure before each climb, and retire it if anything looks off. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
For other small connectors, see our climbing hardware.

Treat the Quickie like any other component in your climbing system. Learn how it is supposed to sit and load from the manufacturer's instructions, practice with it close to the ground, and ask a trainer or experienced climber to check your setup if you have not used one before.

faq.q: Can the Quickie replace all my carabiners?
faq.a: No. It is meant for specific connections. Use rated locking carabiners wherever the instructions call for them.

faq.q: What changed in the V3?
faq.a: Notch updates designs based on field use. Check the current product instructions for the details of this version.

name: Petzl Speedy Link
title: Petzl Speedy Link: Quick Link for Climbing Setups
h1: Petzl Speedy Link Climbing Quick Link
meta: A quick link for climbing setups that need a compact, semi-permanent connection. Where the Petzl Speedy Link fits on a saddle and how to inspect it properly.
tagline: A compact quick link for semi-permanent connections in a climbing setup.
summary: The Petzl Speedy Link is a quick link for climbing setups where a semi-permanent, low-profile connection beats a bulky carabiner. Screw it closed and it stays closed, which makes it a tidy choice for attaching hardware that rarely comes off.
highlights: Low-profile threaded closure
Good for semi-permanent connections
Keeps hardware in place and oriented
Less bulk than a full carabiner

body.h: When a quick link makes sense
p: Quick links shine for connections you set once and leave: attaching a pulley to a saddle, closing a rope bridge setup or holding a device in a fixed position. With no spring gate to snag, they sit flat and behave predictably.
They are slower to open than a carabiner, so they are not the right choice for anything you clip and unclip all day.

They also make sense where a carabiner gate could be pushed open by a limb or another piece of hardware. With the sleeve screwed closed, there is no gate to snag, which can make a quick link the cleaner choice in a crowded spot on the saddle.

A quick link is only as strong as its closure. Screw the sleeve fully closed every time, and check that it stays tight during the day. Look for thread damage, deformation and corrosion. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

Check the rating marked on the link and the manufacturer's instructions before using it in any life-support position. Not every quick link is rated for climbing, and only those that are should go anywhere near your system. Keep general hardware-store links out of your kit altogether.

faq.q: Is a quick link stronger than a carabiner?
faq.a: It depends on the specific products. Read the rating on the link and the instructions, and never use it beyond those limits.

faq.q: Do I need a tool to close it?
faq.a: Follow the manufacturer's instructions. Many are closed firmly by hand; a sleeve that will not stay tight means it is time to replace it.

name: Stainless Steel Twisted Shackle
title: Stainless Steel Twist Shackle for Rigging Setups
meta: A stainless steel twist shackle turns the pin 90 degrees to the bow so blocks and slings line up cleanly. Where it helps in tree rigging and what to check.
tagline: A twisted stainless shackle that turns the connection 90 degrees for cleaner alignment.
summary: A twist shackle has its pin set at 90 degrees to the bow, so hardware connected through it turns a quarter turn. In tree work that helps blocks, slings and eyes line up the way the load wants to run instead of twisting.
highlights: Pin set at 90 degrees to the bow
Corrosion-resistant stainless steel
Helps hardware line up with the load
Useful in rigging and hardware setups
specs: Check the working load marked on the shackle

p: Some hardware connects at the wrong angle. A block hanging from a sling may want to face sideways, or a hook may twist a rope eye. A twist shackle turns the connection a quarter turn so everything lies flat and loads straight.
Stainless steel holds up well in the truck, in wet weather and around bar oil.

Twist shackles are a small piece of hardware, but they solve a real problem. When an eye or hook is loaded at the wrong angle, it twists the rope or sling under load, which adds wear and can make a setup behave unpredictably as the piece comes off the tree.

Only use a shackle with a clearly marked working load, and size it to the job. Rigging loads in tree work can be many times the weight of the piece being lowered, so leave a big margin. Do not use general hardware in a life-support climbing system.
Inspect the pin threads and bow for wear or bending before use. For rigging connectors, also see our hardware range.

Screw the pin fully home every time, and mouse or secure it if the setup could shake it loose. Replace any shackle with a bent bow, stretched pin or damaged threads, and keep stainless and galvanized hardware separate so you always know what is rated for what.

faq.q: Can I climb on this shackle?
faq.a: No. Use only hardware rated for life support in a climbing system.

faq.q: What is a twist shackle used for?
faq.a: To turn a connection 90 degrees so blocks, hooks and eyes line up with the load.

name: DMM XSRE Carabiner
title: DMM XSRE Accessory Carabiner for Racking Gear
meta: The DMM XSRE is a small non-locking accessory carabiner for racking tools and gear on a saddle. What it is for, what it is not for, and how to set up your rack.
tagline: A small DMM accessory carabiner for keeping your saddle rack organized.
summary: The DMM XSRE is a small non-locking accessory carabiner for racking gear on a saddle, gear bag or truck rack. It is light, cleanly made and easy to clip with gloves, which makes it a solid choice for handsaws, slings and spare cord.
highlights: Small, light accessory carabiner
Smooth DMM gate action
Good for organizing saddle gear loops
Not for climbing or life support

p: A tidy rack saves time aloft. Put the things you reach for most on the front loops, keep rescue gear in a fixed spot, and use clips like the XSRE so each item lives in one place. You will stop hunting for the hitch cord you know you brought.
Using a distinct accessory clip for racking also keeps your rated carabiners free for the system.

The XSRE is small enough that you can carry several without noticing the weight. Give each one a job and keep it there: one for the handsaw scabbard, one for spare hitch cord, one for a throw bag. Your hand will learn where everything lives.
Accessory carabiners are not life-support equipment. Never put one into a climbing, rigging or rescue system. For rated connectors, look at the DMM Shadow or our other locking carabiners.

It is also good practice to pick a racking clip that looks different from your rated hardware. If the whole crew knows the small clips are for racking only, nobody grabs one in a hurry to close a system. Retire any accessory clip with a bent gate or sharp edges, since it can still damage slings and rope.

faq.q: Can I use the XSRE in my climbing system?
faq.a: No. Treat it as an accessory clip for racking gear only.

faq.q: What should I clip to it?
faq.a: Light gear such as slings, hitch cords, small pulleys and tool scabbards.

name: Petzl Rollclip Pulley Carabiner
title: Petzl Rollclip Pulley Carabiner for Arborists
meta: The Petzl Rollclip is a roller carabiner with a built-in pulley for hitch tending, hauling and rescue systems. How arborists use it and what to inspect first.
tagline: A carabiner with a built-in pulley for hitch tending, hauls and redirects.
summary: The Petzl Rollclip is a carabiner with a pulley built into the frame, so one piece of hardware does the job of a pulley and a connector. Arborists use the roller carabiner to tend hitches, build quick haul systems and redirect a line.
highlights: Pulley and carabiner in one unit
Reduces bulk on a hitch setup
Handy for mechanical advantage hauls
Fast to clip onto a rope mid-line

p: A Petzl carabiner with a pulley saves a part. Instead of a separate pulley and connector at the bottom of a hitch, the Rollclip clips straight in and lets the rope run over a sheave. That means less clutter and less hardware to cross-load.
It is also quick to clip onto a rope without opening the system, which is useful for building a simple haul with a rope clamp like the Kong Duck.

Rescue kits benefit most. A Rollclip, a rope clamp and a sling cover a lot of ground in an aerial rescue or a stuck-climber situation, and they pack down small enough to live on a saddle every day. Train with the systems you plan to use before you need them.

Check that the sheave turns freely, the gate closes and locks or springs back as designed, and the frame shows no cracks or grooves. Keep it clean, since grit in the sheave wears both the device and your rope. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
Rope wear is a good tell. If the sheave stops turning freely, the rope starts dragging over it and wears faster. Spin it by hand before you climb and clean or retire it if it sticks or wobbles.

faq.q: Can the Rollclip replace a hitch-tending pulley?
faq.a: For many setups, yes. Check that your hitch and rope suit it and follow Petzl's instructions.

faq.q: Is it rated for life support?
faq.a: Check the markings and notice for your specific model and use it only as Petzl describes.

name: Rock Exotica RockX Accessory Carabiner
title: Rock Exotica RockX Accessory Carabiner
meta: The RockX accessory carabiner is a light Rock Exotica clip for racking slings, cords and tools. How to build a clean saddle rack and keep it out of the system.
tagline: A light Rock Exotica clip for racking slings, cords and tools.
summary: The RockX accessory carabiner is a lightweight Rock Exotica clip for holding gear on a saddle, bag or truck rack. It is shaped like the rated hardware climbers already know, but it is meant for lightweight accessories, not for life support.
highlights: Light accessory carabiner from Rock Exotica
Easy to clip and unclip with gloves
Keeps slings, cords and tools organized
Frees up rated connectors for the climbing system
Not for climbing, rigging or rescue loads

p: Every saddle collects small gear: a spare split tail, a rescue pulley, a handsaw scabbard, a few slings and a throw bag. The RockX accessory carabiner gives each of those a home. Clip them to your gear loops and you can find them by feel without looking down.
Rock Exotica makes some of the most respected rated hardware in rope access and tree work, and the RockX carries over the feel of that hardware in a light clip built for lightweight accessories.
Because it is cheap and light, it is easy to keep a handful on the saddle and a few more in the gear bag, so there is always a spare when you add a new piece of kit to the rack.

Start with the gear you reach for most. Handsaw on the side you cut with, lanyard parked where your hand falls naturally, and rescue gear in the same place every day so a groundie or co-climber can find it too.

Use accessory clips for anything that only needs to hang. That keeps your rated locking carabiners free and reduces the chance of a rated connector being treated like a gear hook. When you need a rated locker, look at our auto-locking carabiners.

Separate rescue gear from day-to-day gear on the rack. A dedicated accessory clip that holds a pulley, a sling and a rope clamp together means a co-climber can grab the whole kit at once if you need help.
Think about the order you will need things in an emergency too. Rescue gear should be easy to reach with either hand, and it should not be buried behind your handsaw or a pile of slings.

body.h: Keep it out of the system
p: An accessory carabiner is not personal protective equipment. Never use it to connect a climbing line, lanyard, rigging line or rescue system, even for a moment. A color or shape that differs from your rated hardware helps everyone on the crew tell them apart.
Retire accessory clips that have bent gates or sharp edges, since they can still damage slings and rope.
Accessory clips are handy off the tree too. Hang wet slings and lanyards to dry, keep spare hitch cord bundled in the truck, and clip a small first-aid pouch where everyone knows to look for it.

On the ground, a few accessory clips on the side of a gear bag make it easy to keep rigging slings, spare hitch cord and small pulleys sorted by size. When you pack up at the end of the day, it is easy to see if something is missing.

They also make a handy way to keep a set of ear plugs, a spare pair of safety glasses or a small trauma kit clipped where the whole crew can find them. A minute spent organizing the truck at the start of the week saves a lot of hunting on a busy job site.

faq.q: Can I climb on a RockX accessory carabiner?
faq.a: No. It is for racking lightweight accessories. Use a rated locking carabiner for every life-support connection.

faq.q: What should I hang on it?
faq.a: Slings, hitch cords, small pulleys, tool scabbards and other light gear.

faq.q: Why not just use spare locking carabiners for racking?
faq.a: You can, but accessory clips are lighter and cheaper, and keeping them separate makes it clear which hardware belongs in the system.

name: Petzl Am'D Screw-Lock Carabiner
title: Petzl Am'D Screw-Lock Locking Carabiner
meta: The Petzl Am'D Screw-Lock is a Petzl locking carabiner with an asymmetric D frame for semi-permanent connections. Ratings, best uses and inspection basics.
tagline: Petzl's asymmetric D locker with a screw gate for semi-permanent connections.
summary: The Petzl Am'D Screw-Lock is a Petzl locking carabiner built on the same asymmetric D frame as the auto-locking Am'D, with a manual screw gate. It suits connections you set and leave, such as a pulley on a bridge or a device that stays clipped all day.
highlights: Asymmetric D frame keeps load near the spine
Manual screw gate for semi-permanent connections
Keylock nose slides through eyes
28 kN major-axis rating

body.h: When to pick a screw gate
p: A screw gate is simple and reliable, but it only locks when you lock it. That makes it a good choice for connections you rarely open, and a poor one for connections you open all day. For those, the Am'D Triact-Lock locks itself.
Check your company policy and the applicable standard; many require self-locking connectors in certain positions.

The Am'D frame is the same shape climbers already know from the auto-locking version. The asymmetric D keeps the load close to the spine and leaves a wide end for hitches, rope eyes and pulleys, and the keylock nose slides through sewn eyes without snagging.

Screw the gate closed and check it with a squeeze every time. Vibration and rope movement can work a screw gate loose, so recheck during the day. Look for grit in the threads, rope wear and cracks. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

Clean the threads when they get gritty. Sap and sawdust make a screw gate stiff, which makes it more likely you will leave it partly unlocked. Rinse it in warm water, dry it and retire any carabiner that has taken a hard drop or shows cracks or deep rope grooves.

faq.q: Is a screw-lock carabiner OK for tree climbing?
faq.a: It is used for semi-permanent connections, but many climbers and policies prefer auto-locking gates for anything opened often.

faq.q: What are the ratings?
faq.a: 28 kN major axis, 8 kN minor axis and 7 kN gate open. Confirm the markings on your carabiner.

name: Petzl William Screw-Lock Carabiner
title: Petzl William Screw Lock Carabiner, Large Pear
meta: The Petzl William is a large pear-shaped screw lock carabiner with room for hitches, rope and several connections. Uses, ratings and screw gate habits.
tagline: A large pear-shaped screw lock carabiner with room for rope and multiple connections.
summary: The Petzl William is a large pear-shaped screw lock carabiner with a wide gate and a roomy basket. It holds several connections, takes a fat rope hitch and gives you space to work with gloves on, which is why it shows up in anchors, rescue kits and rigging setups.
highlights: Large pear shape with plenty of room inside
Wide opening for rope, eyes and slings
Screw-lock gate for semi-permanent connections
Keylock nose reduces snagging
Light aluminum body

p: Pear-shaped carabiners give a wide, round end where rope and several connections can sit side by side without binding. The William is one of the larger ones, which makes it handy wherever several things meet: an anchor point, a lowering setup, the master point of a rescue system or a pulley with a sling.
With gloves on and cold hands, the extra room makes clipping faster and reduces the chance of trapping a sling across the gate.

Beyond the tree, the William is handy for building a lowering anchor at the base, holding a block and sling together, or clipping a few slings at a central point for a rescue. Its size makes it easy to see in a pile of gear, which helps on a busy job site.
If you work mostly with gloves, a large carabiner like this is simply easier to handle than a small D.

A screw lock carabiner locks only when you turn the sleeve closed. It is simple, has few parts and is easy to inspect, but it relies on you. Make a habit of screwing it shut, then squeezing the gate to confirm it is locked.

Screw gates suit connections you set and leave. For connections you open many times a day, an auto-locking gate is the safer choice. Compare with the Petzl Am'D Screw-Lock if you want a smaller D shape.
A simple rule many crews use: screw it closed, give it a quarter turn back so it does not bind, then squeeze to check. Do it the same way every time.
If your company policy calls for auto-locking connectors in life-support positions, keep the William for anchors, rigging and rescue setups where a screw gate is allowed.

Pear carabiners have a wide basket, so pay attention to how multiple connections sit. The more the load spreads away from the spine, the lower the strength. Keep loads near the spine and avoid three-way loading unless the manufacturer allows it.
Keep the gate away from limbs and other hardware, and watch that the sleeve does not unscrew as rope runs past it.

Check thread condition, gate spring and the inside of the basket for rope grooves. Rinse out sap and grit, dry it, and retire any carabiner that has been dropped hard or shows cracks or deep wear. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

Pay special attention to the inside of the basket where rope runs over it. Large carabiners used for lowering or as a master point often see more rope movement than a typical climbing connector, so grooves can develop faster. A groove with a sharp edge can damage rope, so retire it before that point.

faq.q: What is a screw lock carabiner?
faq.a: A carabiner with a threaded sleeve on the gate that you turn by hand to lock it closed.

faq.q: How strong is the Petzl William?
faq.a: It is rated 27 kN major axis, 8 kN minor axis and 7 kN gate open. Always check the markings on your carabiner.

faq.q: Screw lock or auto-lock for climbing?
faq.a: Auto-locking gates are preferred for connections you open often. Screw locks are fine for semi-permanent connections if you lock and check them every time.

name: SMC Large Heat Treated Steel Screw Locking Carabiner
title: SMC Extra Large Heavy Duty Steel Carabiner
h1: SMC Extra Large Heavy Duty Steel Screw Locking Carabiner
meta: An extra large heavy duty carabiner in heat-treated steel from SMC, with a screw gate and room for several connections. Best rigging uses and inspection tips.
tagline: An extra large, heat-treated steel screw-lock carabiner for heavy-duty connections.
summary: This SMC large steel carabiner is an extra large heavy duty carabiner for connections that see abuse: rigging, anchors and setups where several slings or a thick rope have to fit. Heat-treated steel resists wear from rope and hardware far better than aluminum.
highlights: Heat-treated steel for wear resistance
Large opening and basket
Screw-lock gate
Ratings marked on the spine

p: Steel carabiners weigh more than aluminum, but they shrug off the grooving that rigging rope and steel hardware cause. That makes them a smart choice for rigging connections, anchors and gear that sits in the truck bed between jobs.
The large size gives room for bigger rope, several slings or a block and a sling together.

Heat treatment hardens the steel so it resists wear, which is why steel carabiners last longer on rigging lines that carry grit and sap. The trade-off is weight, so most climbers keep steel off the saddle and in the rigging bag.

Read the ratings on the spine and keep loads within them, remembering that rigging forces can far exceed the weight of a piece of wood. Lock the screw gate and check it every time. Retire it if it shows cracks, bending or deep wear. For life-support use, confirm the carabiner is rated for it and follow the applicable standard. See more in screw gate carabiners.

When stacking several connections in the basket, keep the loads near the spine and avoid three-way loading unless the manufacturer allows it. Screw the gate closed, then squeeze the gate to confirm it is locked, and recheck after rope has been running past it.

faq.q: Is steel stronger than aluminum?
faq.a: Steel carabiners are usually stronger and more wear resistant, but always go by the ratings marked on the carabiner.

faq.q: Is this good for rigging?
faq.a: Steel carabiners are common in rigging connections. Keep within the marked ratings and size hardware for the expected forces.

name: Aluminum Double Locking Snap Hook
title: Aluminum Double Locking Snap Hook for Lanyards
meta: A light aluminum snap hook with a double locking gate for lanyards and positioning gear. Where it fits, how it compares to steel, and what to inspect each day.
tagline: A lighter double locking snap for lanyards and positioning gear.
summary: This aluminum snap hook has a double locking gate: you press the keeper and then open the gate, so it cannot be opened by a single push. Lighter than steel, it suits lanyard ends and positioning setups where weight adds up over a day.
highlights: Double locking gate needs two actions to open
Lighter than an equivalent steel snap
Easy to operate with one gloved hand
Good fit for lanyard ends

p: A double locking snap closes and locks automatically, and opening it takes two deliberate actions. That makes it hard for a branch, rope or D-ring to open it by accident, which is why snaps like this are common on lanyards and positioning gear.
Aluminum cuts weight compared with steel, which you notice at the end of a long day on spurs.

Snap hooks also hold their orientation better than a carabiner on a sewn or spliced lanyard end. They are less likely to twist and cross-load against a D-ring when you lean back on a stem, which matters when you are on spurs and working with both hands.

Aluminum wears faster than steel where it rubs against steel hardware or wire core lanyards. Check for grooves, sharp edges, a sticky keeper and a gate that does not snap shut. Make sure the snap is compatible with the D-rings on your saddle. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
Compare with the steel locking rope snap.
If you use the snap with a wire core flipline, keep an eye on where the wire rubs. Aluminum grooves faster under steel, and a sharp groove can damage rope or slings that run through it later.

faq.q: Aluminum or steel snap?
faq.a: Aluminum is lighter; steel resists wear better around wire core and steel hardware. Pick based on how you work and inspect accordingly.

faq.q: What is a double locking snap?
faq.a: A snap hook that locks itself when closed and needs two separate actions to open.

name: Petzl Eashook Open Rope Snap
title: Petzl Eashook Open Rope Snap Connector
meta: The Petzl Eashook Open is a wide-opening aluminum snap connector for lanyards and anchor points. How it works, where arborists use it, and how to inspect it.
tagline: A wide-opening Petzl snap connector for lanyards and large anchors.
summary: The Petzl Eashook Open is a wide-opening aluminum connector designed for lanyards that clip around large anchors and structures. It locks automatically and opens with one hand, which suits work where you clip and unclip often.
highlights: Wide gate opening for larger anchors
Automatic locking gate
One-handed operation
Aluminum body keeps weight down

p: The Eashook family is built for lanyard ends. The Open version has a large gate opening, so it clips around bigger hardware, rebar-type anchors and structures where a standard carabiner will not fit.
In tree work it often ends up on the end of a positioning lanyard or on a bucket truck setup. Check the instructions to confirm the configuration you plan to use.

The hook shape keeps the connector oriented on the end of a sewn lanyard, so it stays ready to clip as you move. The wide opening is also easier to clip around an anchor when you are wearing heavy gloves.

Make sure the gate closes and locks automatically every time, and that the release works smoothly. Look for wear, cracks and deformation. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

Keep the release mechanism clean. Grit and sap make it stiff, which can stop the gate from closing fully. Rinse it in warm water, dry it, and test the action before the next job. Retire it after a hard drop or if it shows cracks or deformation.

faq.q: Can I use the Eashook Open on my climbing system?
faq.a: Use it only as Petzl describes, typically on lanyard ends. Read the notice for approved uses.

faq.q: How is it different from a carabiner?
faq.a: It has a larger opening and a lanyard-friendly shape designed to stay oriented on a sewn end.

name: Steel Locking Rope Snap
title: Steel Locking Rope Snap for Lanyards and Lines
meta: A steel locking rope snap for spliced lanyards and climbing lines. Why arborists like steel snaps, how a locking keeper works, and what to inspect before work.
tagline: A tough steel locking snap for spliced lanyards and lines.
summary: A steel locking rope snap is the classic hardware on the end of a spliced lanyard or climbing line. The locking keeper must be pressed before the gate opens, and steel stands up to the wear that wire core and saddle D-rings dish out.
highlights: Steel body for wear resistance
Locking keeper prevents accidental opening
Classic choice for spliced lanyard ends
Swivel-free, low-profile design

p: Snaps on lanyards rub against D-rings, wire core and bark all day. Steel takes that abuse far better than aluminum, so a steel locking rope snap is a good choice for gear that sees hard daily use.
The snap is usually spliced or sewn onto the rope by a qualified splicer. Do not tie your own hardware onto life-support rope unless you are trained to do so.

Steel snaps also handle being dragged across bark, dropped in the truck bed and clipped against D-rings thousands of times. They are heavier than aluminum, but on gear that sees daily abuse that weight buys longer service life.

Check that the gate and keeper snap closed on their own, the hinge pin is tight, and there is no rust pitting, cracks or wear. Make sure the snap is compatible with your saddle D-rings. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
For a lighter option, see the aluminum double locking snap hook.

Keep the hinge and keeper free of sap and grit. A sticky keeper is the most common problem and it means the snap may not lock fully. Rinse it, dry it and test it before you trust it, and retire any snap that will not close and lock cleanly.

faq.q: Can I put this snap on my own lanyard?
faq.a: Hardware on life-support rope should be spliced or sewn by a qualified person and meet the applicable standard.

faq.q: Steel or aluminum?
faq.a: Steel lasts longer under wear; aluminum is lighter. Both need daily inspection.

name: Steel Locking Carabiner
title: Steel Carabiners for Rigging and Hard-Wear Use
meta: Steel carabiners hold up to rope wear, steel hardware and truck-bed abuse far better than aluminum. When an arborist should choose steel and how to inspect it.
tagline: Tough steel locking carabiners for rigging and hard-wearing connections.
summary: A steel carabiner is the tough choice for connections that grind against rope, steel hardware and bark. Steel carabiners weigh more than aluminum but last much longer where wear is the main enemy, especially in rigging.
highlights: Steel resists rope grooving
Good for rigging and anchor connections
Locking gate
Ratings marked on the spine

p: Rigging lines carry grit and sap that slowly saw grooves into aluminum. A steel carabiner shrugs that off. Steel is also a good fit for anchors, lowering setups, block connections and any hardware that rides around in the truck between jobs.
On the saddle, weight matters more, so most climbers keep aluminum for their personal system and save steel for rigging and anchors.

Steel is also easier to live with in the truck. It does not mind being tossed in a bin with blocks, slings and rigging rope, and it shrugs off the knocks that would dent or score an aluminum carabiner.

Read the ratings on the spine, check gate action and locking, and look for cracks, bending and rust pitting. Rigging forces can be far higher than the weight of the piece, so size hardware with a generous margin. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
For a larger option, see the SMC large steel carabiner.

Choose a size that fits the rope and slings you rig with. A carabiner that is too small forces sharp bends in rope and slings, which lowers their strength, while one that is too large can let connections shift around inside the basket.

faq.q: Is a steel carabiner stronger than aluminum?
faq.a: Usually, but always go by the ratings marked on the specific carabiner.

faq.q: Should I climb on steel carabiners?
faq.a: You can if they are rated for life support, but most climbers prefer lighter aluminum for their personal system.

name: Weaver Chainsaw Strap with Snap
title: Weaver Chainsaw Belt Strap with Snap
h1: Weaver Chainsaw Belt Strap with Snap
meta: The Weaver chainsaw strap with snap, often called a chainsaw belt, keeps your saw hung from the saddle while you climb. How to set it up and inspect it.
tagline: A simple strap and snap for hanging a saw from your saddle.
summary: The Weaver chainsaw strap with snap, often searched as a chainsaw belt, attaches your saw to your saddle so it hangs out of the way while you climb and stays with you if you drop it. It is a simple, durable way to carry a top-handle saw aloft.
highlights: Keeps the saw attached to the saddle
Snap clips to a saddle ring
Durable Weaver construction
Lets the saw hang out of the way
specs: Attaching a saw to the saddle

p: The strap goes on the saw's lanyard ring and the snap clips to a saddle ring set aside for the saw. When you are not cutting, the saw hangs at your side, out of the way of your climbing line and lanyard.
Keep the saw away from your climbing system and never clip the saw strap to a life-support attachment point.

Hanging the saw from a strap also means you do not have to hold it while you reposition or climb a few feet. That frees both hands for your lanyard and climbing line, which is where they should be when you move.
Set the strap length so the saw hangs where it does not swing into your legs or your lanyard, and where you can reach it quickly without looking down.

Inspect the strap for cuts, abrasion and chain damage, and the snap for wear. A strap that has been nicked by the chain should be replaced. Climbing with a chainsaw requires training and the right PPE, including chainsaw-rated protection where applicable. More options are in chainsaw lanyards.
Clean sawdust and bar oil off the strap at the end of the day, and let it dry before storing. Oil and fuel can weaken webbing over time.

faq.q: Is a chainsaw strap life-support gear?
faq.a: No. It holds the saw, not the climber. Never clip it into your climbing system.

faq.q: Strap or bungee lanyard?
faq.a: A strap is simple and tough; a bungee lanyard gives more reach. Pick what suits how you cut.

name: 2-in-1 Wire Core Lanyard
title: 2 in 1 Lanyard for Tree Climbing, Wire Core
meta: A 2 in 1 lanyard for tree climbing pairs a wire core flipline with a second leg for passing limbs while tied in. How it works, who needs one and safety notes.
tagline: A wire core lanyard with a second leg for repositioning and staying tied in.
summary: A 2 in 1 lanyard for tree climbing gives you two connection points in one piece of gear, with wire core where cut resistance counts. It lets you keep one leg around the stem while you move the other past a limb, so you stay tied in through the whole move.
highlights: Two legs for staying tied in while passing limbs
Wire core for cut resistance near the saw
Fewer separate lanyards on the saddle
Common choice for removals and spar work

p: Passing limbs on a spar is when climbers are most likely to get caught out. With a 2 in 1 lanyard you set the second leg above or below the limb before releasing the first, so you are always tied in twice during the move.
The wire core adds cut resistance, but it is not chainsaw proof. Keep the saw away from any lanyard.

Having both legs on one lanyard also cuts clutter. There is one piece to manage on the saddle instead of two, and less chance of the second lanyard catching on limbs or tangling with your climbing line as you work down a spar.

Choose a length that suits the stems you work on and pair it with a good adjuster. Inspect the rope cover, wire core and splices for damage, kinks and broken strands, and the snaps for wear. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
Compare with the 2-in-1 wire core flipline kit.
Store it coiled loosely, away from fuel and bar oil, and never leave a wire core lanyard kinked under weight. A sharp kink can damage the core in ways that are hard to see from outside.

faq.q: Is a wire core lanyard cut proof?
faq.a: No. It resists cuts better than plain rope but can still be cut by a chainsaw.

faq.q: Who needs a 2-in-1 lanyard?
faq.a: Climbers doing spar work and removals where they need to stay tied in while passing limbs.

name: Adjustable Pole Strap
title: Pole Climbing Straps: Adjustable Pole Strap
meta: An adjustable pole strap for climbers on poles and spars. How pole climbing straps work, how to fit and adjust one, and the checks to make before every climb.
tagline: An adjustable strap for positioning on poles and smooth spars.
summary: This adjustable pole strap is one of the simplest pole climbing straps you can buy: a sturdy strap with snaps that wraps the pole and clips to your saddle D-rings. It holds you in position on spurs while you work with both hands.
highlights: Adjusts to different pole and spar sizes
Snaps clip to saddle D-rings
Simple, durable construction
Good backup or utility positioning strap

p: A pole strap goes around the pole and clips to both side D-rings on your saddle. You lean back against it, your spurs hold your feet, and you have both hands free to work. Adjusting the length lets you choose how far back you sit.
On trees, a flipline with a rope or wire core is usually a better choice because of limbs and the saw. Pole straps are best on smooth poles and spars.

Pole straps are also handy as a utility positioning strap on large, clean spars where you do not need to pass limbs. The flat strap spreads load around the stem, which is easier on bark than a thin rope.

Inspect the strap for cuts, abrasion and stitching damage, and the snaps for wear and correct closure. Make sure the snaps are compatible with your D-rings. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
For tree work, see our fliplines and lanyards.

Keep the strap away from sharp edges, climbing spikes and the saw. Wash off mud and sap with mild soap and water, dry it out of direct sun, and retire it if the stitching or webbing shows damage. Store it away from fuel, oil and chemicals.

faq.q: Can I use a pole strap in trees?
faq.a: It can work on clean spars, but fliplines handle limbs and cutting better.

faq.q: How do I size it?
faq.a: Choose an adjustment range that fits the poles you climb, with enough length to lean back comfortably.

name: 2-in-1 Wire Core Flipline Kit
title: 2-in-1 Wire Core Flip Line Kit with Adjuster
meta: A 2-in-1 steel core flip line kit with adjuster for spar work and removals. How the two legs keep you tied in, what comes in the kit, and how to inspect it.
tagline: A ready-to-climb wire core flip line kit with two legs and an adjuster.
summary: This 2-in-1 wire core flip line kit gives you a complete positioning setup with two legs, so you can stay tied in while passing limbs on a spar. The steel core flip line adds cut resistance where the saw works close to the rope.
highlights: Complete kit, ready to set up
Two legs for passing limbs while tied in
Steel core flip line for cut resistance
Adjuster for one-handed length changes

p: Buying a flipline kit saves matching parts yourself. The lanyard, adjuster and hardware are chosen to work together, and you can climb with it as soon as you have read the instructions and set it up correctly.
The 2-in-1 layout means a second leg is always ready when you reach a limb on a removal.
Kits also make it easier to replace a worn flipline with the same setup you are used to. Your hands already know the adjuster and the length, so there is no relearning on the stem.

Inspect the cover for cuts and glazing, feel for broken wire strands and kinks, and check the splices and snaps. Retire the flipline if the core is damaged. Wire core resists cuts but is not chainsaw proof. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
Need a single-leg version? See the 1/2 in wire core flipline.
Never store a flipline kinked, wet or under weight. Hang or coil it loosely in a dry place away from fuel, oil and sharp hardware. Clean sap from the adjuster so it keeps gripping consistently.

faq.q: What is a flip line?
faq.a: A positioning lanyard that wraps the trunk and connects to the side D-rings of your saddle so you can lean back and work.

faq.q: Why steel core?
faq.a: The wire core resists accidental cuts better than plain rope, though it can still be cut by a chainsaw.

name: Petzl Grillon Hook Work Positioning Lanyard
title: Petzl Grillon Hook Adjustable Positioning Lanyard
h1: Petzl Grillon Hook Work Positioning Lanyard
meta: The Petzl Grillon Hook is an adjustable positioning lanyard with a hook connector. How arborists use the Grillon, how it adjusts, and what to inspect first.
tagline: An adjustable work-positioning lanyard with a hook connector for quick anchors.
summary: The Petzl Grillon Hook is an adjustable work-positioning lanyard with a cam adjuster at one end and a wide-opening hook at the other. Pull the free end to shorten, ease the adjuster to lengthen, and you can set your position on a stem, pole or structure with one hand.
highlights: Adjustable length with one-handed control
Hook connector clips around larger anchors
Simple, proven Petzl adjuster design
Works for tree, pole and structure positioning
Available in several lengths
specs: Hook, plus carabiner at the adjuster

p: The Grillon is a rope lanyard with a cam adjuster that grips the rope under load. Pull the free end and you shorten up; operate the handle on the adjuster and you lengthen in a controlled way. It is quick and smooth, even with gloves on.

The Hook version adds a wide-opening hook connector at the far end of the lanyard, so it clips around bigger anchors and hardware than a standard carabiner can. That makes it popular for bucket and pole work as well as climbing.

Because the adjuster sits at your hip, length changes happen right where your hands are. That makes it easy to snug up as you reach a stem, ease off to lean back for a cut, and take up slack again when you move.

In trees, many climbers use the Grillon as a secondary positioning lanyard during pruning and climbing, choking a limb or wrapping the stem to free up both hands. Arborists who cut close to the lanyard often prefer a wire core flipline or a tree-specific lanyard such as the Petzl Zillon.
The lanyard rope is not cut resistant. Keep the saw away from it, and use a wire core lanyard or follow your crew's cutting procedure when making cuts near your tie-in.
A quick habit that helps: before each cut, look at where your lanyard runs and where the bar will exit the wood, and move one or the other if they are close.

Shorter lanyards are easier to manage and stay out of the way. Longer ones let you wrap bigger stems and reach around obstacles. Think about the trunk sizes you usually work and the way you hang the spare tail on your saddle.
The free tail of a long Grillon can be stowed in a small bag or clipped to a gear loop so it does not tangle with your climbing line.
If you work on poles or bucket trucks as well as trees, the hook end makes the Grillon easy to clip around crossarms and large structures where a standard carabiner might not fit.

Check the adjuster for wear on the cam, smooth action of the handle and a working spring. Inspect the rope for cuts, glazing and stiff spots, especially near the adjuster, and the hook for wear and correct closure. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

Wash the rope in cool water with a mild soap if it gets heavily soiled, let it dry out of direct sun, and store the lanyard loosely coiled in a gear bag away from fuel and chemicals. Keep a note of when it went into service so you know when to look closely at retirement.

faq.q: What is the Petzl Grillon used for?
faq.a: It is an adjustable work-positioning lanyard for holding a worker in position on trees, poles and structures. It is not a fall arrest lanyard.

faq.q: Grillon or Zillon for tree work?
faq.a: Both are adjustable lanyards. The Zillon is designed with tree care in mind; the Grillon is a general work-positioning lanyard. Pick based on how you work.

faq.q: Can I replace the rope on a Grillon?
faq.a: Petzl offers replacement lanyards for some versions. Follow Petzl's instructions and use only approved parts.

faq.q: Is the Grillon chainsaw resistant?
faq.a: No. The rope can be cut by a saw. Keep the saw away from it or use a wire core flipline when cutting near your lanyard.

name: Petzl Zillon Lanyard
title: Petzl Zillon Adjustable Lanyard for Tree Care
meta: The Petzl Zillon is an adjustable work-positioning lanyard built for tree care, with a smooth adjuster for one-handed control. Uses, setup and inspection.
tagline: Petzl's adjustable positioning lanyard built for tree care and all-day spar work.
summary: The Petzl Zillon is an adjustable work-positioning lanyard built with tree care in mind. Its adjuster lets you shorten and lengthen the lanyard with one hand, so you can set your position on a stem or limb and get back to work fast.
highlights: Adjuster designed for tree care positioning
Smooth one-handed lengthening and shortening
Sewn termination at the far end
Several lengths to suit different stems
Pairs well with a wire core flipline for cutting

p: The Zillon handles the thing positioning lanyards do all day: lean back, shorten, ease off, lean again. The adjuster grips firmly when loaded and releases with a controlled pull on the handle, so you can creep out a few inches at a time without jerking.
Climbers use it to choke a limb while pruning, to set a second point while limb walking, and to hold position on a spar while they make cuts below their feet.

The adjuster also works well for limb walking. As you move out on a limb, you can keep the lanyard snug as a second point of contact and let out length in small steps, which keeps you balanced and tied in at the same time.

Both are Petzl adjustable lanyards with a cam adjuster. The Zillon is made for tree care, with an adjuster and rope chosen for the way arborists use a lanyard. The Petzl Grillon Hook is a general work-positioning lanyard with a hook connector that suits poles, buckets and structures.
If you mostly climb trees, the Zillon is the more natural fit. If you split time between poles, buckets and trees, the Grillon Hook may be more versatile.
Both are proven designs, so the choice comes down to how and where you work.

A rope lanyard is not cut resistant. On removals, many climbers run the Zillon as their working lanyard and add a wire core flipline whenever they cut near their tie-in, or switch to the flipline for the cutting phase.
Keep the saw on the opposite side from the lanyard and keep your body and lanyard out of the cut path.
Practice the switch between lanyard and flipline on the ground before you need to do it at height, so it becomes routine.
Clear communication with your ground crew matters here too, so everyone knows when you are about to cut and where the piece will land.

Clean sap and grit from the adjuster, check cam teeth and handle action, and inspect the rope for cuts, glazing or stiff areas, particularly near the adjuster and termination. Retire the lanyard if you find damage. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
Wash the rope with cool water and mild soap if it gets heavily soiled, and dry it out of direct sun. Store the lanyard loosely coiled in a gear bag away from fuel and chemicals.
Keep a note of when the lanyard went into service, and follow Petzl's guidance on retirement. A lanyard that has held a hard load or been nicked by a saw should come out of service right away.

faq.q: What is the Petzl Zillon?
faq.a: An adjustable work-positioning lanyard designed for tree care, with a cam adjuster for one-handed length changes.

faq.q: Can I replace the Zillon rope?
faq.a: Petzl offers replacement lanyards for the Zillon. Use only the approved replacement and follow the instructions.

faq.q: Is the Zillon chainsaw resistant?
faq.a: No. Keep the saw away from it and use a wire core flipline when cutting near your lanyard.

faq.q: What length should I buy?
faq.a: Pick a length that wraps the stems you usually work with room to adjust. Many climbers own a shorter and a longer lanyard.

name: Magnetic Lanyard Management System
title: Magnetic Lanyard Management System for Saddles
meta: A magnetic lanyard management system parks your lanyard snap on your saddle so it is out of the way but easy to grab. How it works and where to mount it.
tagline: A magnetic holder that parks your lanyard on the saddle, ready to grab.
summary: This magnetic lanyard management system parks the end of your lanyard on your saddle with a strong magnet, so it stays out of the way while you climb and comes off with one quick pull. No more lanyards dragging through the canopy or snagging on limbs.
highlights: Magnet holds the lanyard end in place
Quick one-handed release
Keeps lanyards from snagging
Mounts on the saddle

p: A lanyard hanging loose snags on limbs, tangles with your climbing line and gets in the way of the saw. A magnetic lanyard holder keeps the snap parked where your hand expects it, so you grab it, wrap, clip and get on with the job.
It is a small change that makes a long day of spar work smoother.

It also helps on the ground. A lanyard that stays parked on the saddle does not drag through mud and sawdust as you walk to the base of the tree, so it stays cleaner and lasts longer. And when you need it in a hurry, it is right where your hand expects it.

Mount it where you naturally reach and where it will not interfere with your bridge or D-rings. It is a storage device only and holds no load, so never use it as an attachment point. Check that magnets and mounting stay secure. For lanyards themselves, see rope lanyards.

Keep the magnet clean of metal shavings and chain filings, which build up over time and weaken the hold. Wipe it down when you clean your saddle and check the mount for loose stitching or fasteners. Remember that anything clipped to your saddle should be checked as part of your normal pre-climb inspection.

faq.q: Will the magnet hold a carabiner?
faq.a: It is designed to hold lanyard hardware made of magnetic metal. Aluminum hardware will not stick to a magnet.

faq.q: Is it a life-support component?
faq.a: No. It is only for storing the lanyard end.

name: Petzl Micrograb Lanyard Add-On Kit
title: Petzl Micrograb Lanyard Kit with Rope Grab
h1: Petzl Micrograb Rope Grab Lanyard Kit
meta: The Petzl Micrograb lanyard kit pairs a Petzl rope grab adjuster with lanyard rope to build an adjustable positioning lanyard. Contents and inspection tips.
tagline: A ready kit that pairs the Micrograb adjuster with lanyard rope.
summary: This kit pairs the Petzl Micrograb rope grab adjuster with a length of lanyard rope, giving you an adjustable work-positioning lanyard without sourcing parts yourself. It is a light alternative to a wire core flipline for pruning and general climbing.
highlights: Micrograb rope grab adjuster
Matched lanyard rope
Light alternative to wire core
One-handed adjustment

p: The Micrograb is only as good as the rope it runs on. A kit takes the guesswork out by matching the adjuster to a compatible rope, so you can set it up as Petzl shows and climb.
Rope lanyards are lighter and gentler on bark than wire core, which suits pruning and climbs where you are not cutting near the lanyard.

Kits are also handy as a second lanyard. Many climbers run a wire core flipline for cutting and a light rope lanyard like this for pruning, limb walking and choking a limb for a second point of contact.

Check cam wear, the spring and the body of the Micrograb, and inspect the rope for cuts, glazing and stiff spots. A rope lanyard is not cut resistant. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
Want just the device? See the Petzl Micrograb lanyard adjuster.
Keep the lanyard rope away from fuel and bar oil, and let it dry after wet days before storing it. If the rope gets glazed or stiff near the adjuster, it is time to replace it.

faq.q: What does the kit include?
faq.a: The Micrograb adjuster and lanyard rope. Check the listing for the exact contents and length.

faq.q: Can I use it while cutting?
faq.a: The rope is not cut resistant. Use a wire core flipline when cutting near your lanyard.

name: 1/2 in Wire Core Flipline
title: 1/2 in Wire Core Flip Line for Tree Climbing
meta: A 1/2 in wire core flip line for spar work, removals and spur climbing. How a flipline works, how to pick a length, and the checks to make before every climb.
tagline: A half-inch wire core flipline for spur climbing and removals.
summary: This 1/2 in wire core flip line is a classic positioning lanyard for spur climbing and removals. The steel core gives cut resistance, and the half-inch rope gives a solid grip in an adjuster or hitch.
highlights: Wire core for cut resistance
1/2 in rope suits common adjusters
Classic choice for removals
Spliced snap end (see listing)

p: The flipline wraps the trunk and connects to both side D-rings on your saddle, usually through an adjuster on one side. You lean back on it, set your spurs and work with both hands. As you climb, you flip it up the trunk, which is where the name comes from.
Choose a length that wraps the biggest stems you work with enough tail to adjust.

Half-inch is a common diameter for fliplines because it gives a good grip in a hand and in common adjusters, while staying manageable on the saddle. A wire core flipline also slides around a rough trunk well, which makes flipping up the stem easier.

Check the rope cover for cuts and wear, feel along the core for kinks and broken strands, and inspect splices and snaps. Wire core resists cuts but can still be cut. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
Need two legs? See the 2-in-1 wire core flipline kit.
Store the flipline coiled loosely in a dry place, away from fuel and chemicals, and never leave it kinked or under weight. Kinks can damage the core in ways that are hard to see from the outside.

faq.q: What length flipline do I need?
faq.a: Long enough to wrap the largest trunks you climb with room to adjust. Many climbers carry a mid-length and a long one.

faq.q: Can a chainsaw cut a wire core flipline?
faq.a: Yes. Wire core is more cut resistant than rope, not cut proof.

name: ART Ropeguide Twinline
title: ART Ropeguide Twinline Friction Saver
meta: The ART Ropeguide Twinline is a roller friction saver that protects the tree and your climbing rope at the tie-in point. How it works and how to inspect it.
tagline: A roller friction saver from ART that protects bark and rope at the tie-in.
summary: The ART Ropeguide Twinline is a roller friction saver that sets at the tie-in and lets your climbing rope run over rollers instead of grinding across bark. It protects the cambium, keeps rope wear down and makes advancing your system smoother.
