highlights: Rollers reduce friction at the tie-in
Protects bark and cambium
Less wear on the climbing rope
Twinline design from ART

p: Climbing directly over a branch wears the bark and your rope, and adds friction that makes advancing harder. A friction saver like the ART Ropeguide puts hardware between the rope and the tree. Rollers keep the rope running freely, so you spend energy climbing, not fighting friction.
ART is known for engineered climbing gear, and the Ropeguide line is built for the way climbers actually set and retrieve tie-ins.

The Twinline layout also helps when advancing or adjusting a tie-in. With the rope running over rollers, it slides through easily, so you spend less effort taking up slack and less time fighting friction at the top of the climb.

Set it on a sound, appropriately sized anchor and follow ART's instructions for configuration and retrieval. Inspect the rollers for free movement, check the sling and hardware for wear, and keep it clean. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
Compare it with simpler options in friction savers.

Clean the rollers after sappy jobs. Pitch and grit stop them turning freely and add friction back into the system. If a roller sticks, wobbles or shows wear, stop using it until it has been fixed or replaced.

faq.q: Can I retrieve the Ropeguide from the ground?
faq.a: Many friction savers are retrievable with the right setup. Follow ART's instructions for your configuration.

faq.q: Does it work with SRS and MRS?
faq.a: Check ART's instructions for the configurations the Ropeguide is approved for.

name: CMI Anchor Sling
title: CMI Anchor Sling: Climbing Sling for Tie-Ins
meta: The CMI anchor sling is a webbing climbing sling for setting anchors around stems and limbs. How arborists use it, how to choose a length and how to inspect it.
tagline: A tough webbing anchor sling for setting tie-ins and anchors around stems and limbs.
summary: The CMI anchor sling is a sewn webbing climbing sling for building anchors around stems, limbs and structures. Wrap it, clip both ends and you have a solid anchor for a climbing line, rigging point or rescue system.
highlights: Sewn webbing anchor sling
Quick to set around stems and limbs
Useful for climbing tie-ins, rigging and rescue
Protects rope from bark at the anchor
Packs small on a saddle or in a bag

p: An anchor sling gives you a clean, strong attachment point where a branch union or a basal tie-in would be awkward or hard on the tree. You wrap the sling around a sound stem or limb, clip the ends with a locking carabiner, and attach your climbing line, a pulley or a rigging block.
Compared with tying your rope directly around a limb, a sling saves wear on the rope and makes the anchor easier to retrieve and inspect.

Slings also give you a clean way to choose exactly where your anchor sits. Instead of relying on a crotch that may pinch the rope, you can pick a sound section of stem and place the sling right where you want your tie-in.

body.h: Climbing sling uses on a tree job
p: Climbers use slings for a lot more than tie-ins. They make quick redirects, choke a limb for a positioning point, build a basal anchor for SRS, and give a rescuer a fast attachment point to a stem.
Many climbers carry one or two slings on the saddle at all times, alongside a pulley and a rope clamp like the Kong Duck, so they can build a simple rescue system without going back to the truck.
Practice building these setups on the ground first, so that rigging a sling at height is quick and the result is tidy and easy to check.

Measure the stems you usually anchor to. A sling has to wrap the stem with enough length left over for the ends to meet at a narrow angle. Wide angles between the legs multiply the load on each leg and on the carabiner, so a longer sling is often the safer choice for big trunks.
Short slings are handy for small limbs and quick redirects; long ones for basal anchors and big spars.
When you are unsure, carry a longer sling. It can always be doubled or wrapped twice around a smaller stem, while a short sling cannot be made longer.

Webbing is vulnerable to cuts, abrasion, heat and chemicals such as bar oil solvents and fuel. Check the whole length and the stitching before each use and retire the sling if you find cuts, fuzzing, stiffness, discoloration or damaged stitching. Keep it away from the saw and from sharp edges. Life-support gear has to meet the applicable standard and the manufacturer's instructions, get inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

Store slings in a dry bag away from fuel and oil, and do not leave them in the sun for long periods, since UV exposure weakens webbing over time. Keep a note of when each sling went into service, and wash heavily soiled slings in cool water with mild soap, letting them air dry in the shade.

faq.q: What is an anchor sling?
faq.a: A sewn loop or length of webbing used to create an attachment point around a stem, limb or structure.

faq.q: Can I use a climbing sling for rigging?
faq.a: Only if it is rated for the forces involved. Rigging loads can be very high, so most crews use dedicated rigging slings.

faq.q: How long should my sling be?
faq.a: Long enough to wrap your usual anchor stems with a narrow angle between the legs. Wider angles increase the load on each leg.

faq.q: When should I retire a sling?
faq.a: Retire it if it shows cuts, heavy abrasion, heat damage, chemical contamination or damaged stitching, or follow the manufacturer's retirement guidance.

name: Buckingham Haul Bag
title: Buckingham Haul Bag for Climbing Gear
meta: The Buckingham haul bag keeps climbing rope, saddles and hardware together and off the ground. What fits inside, how it carries and how to keep gear in shape.
tagline: A tough haul bag to keep rope, saddle and hardware together on the job.
summary: The Buckingham haul bag is a durable bag for carrying climbing rope, saddles and hardware from the truck to the tree. A good haul bag keeps gear clean, dry and organized, and it protects your life-support equipment from the sun, fuel and chain oil in the truck bed.
highlights: Durable construction for daily use
Room for rope, saddle and hardware
Keeps gear off the ground
Carry handles for truck-to-tree trips

p: Rope and slings left loose in the truck pick up grit, fuel, bar oil and UV damage, all of which shorten their life. A Buckingham climbing bag gives everything a home, so you know what you have and it stays clean between jobs.
On site, the bag keeps gear off wet ground and sawdust while you set up.
A bag with a stiff base also keeps rope from spilling out into the truck. Rope that stays together is quicker to set up and less likely to get kinked, cut or tangled.

Keep rope flaked or bagged on its own, hardware in a pouch, and the saddle on top so it is not crushed. Do not store fuel, chainsaw chains or chemicals in the same bag. Air everything out after wet days. For more options, see gear bags.
Clean out sawdust and bark that collect in the bottom of the bag. They hold moisture and carry grit back into your rope and hardware. Turn the bag out every few weeks and let it dry in the shade.
Give each crew member a bag with their own gear inside. When every climber knows their kit is complete and inspected, setup on the job is faster and nothing gets borrowed and forgotten.

faq.q: What fits in a haul bag?
faq.a: Typically a climbing rope, saddle, lanyards and hardware. Check the listing for size.

faq.q: Can I store wet rope in it?
faq.a: Dry rope and gear before storing them for long periods to avoid mildew and damage.
